title: Indexed Arrays: Ordered Lists 📋
description: Create and use numeric‑index arrays to store collections of values.

slides.title: What is an Array? 🗄️
slides.content:
## A List with Numbered Slots

An **indexed array** is a variable that holds multiple values, each accessible by a numeric index (starting at 0).

Think of it as a row of lockers. Locker 0 holds the first item, locker 1 the second, and so on.

In Bash, arrays can be created on the fly without declaration, but it's clearer to use `declare -a`.

quizData.question: Which syntax creates an indexed array called `colors`?

slides.title: Accessing Array Elements 📍
slides.content:
## By Index

- Single element: `${array[index]}`
- All elements: `${array[@]}` or `${array[*]}`
- Number of elements: `${#array[@]}`
- Length of a specific element: `${#array[index]}`

Indices are zero‑based. You can also assign to a specific index: `array[3]=dog`.

slides.title: Array Access Examples
slides.codeSnippet:
names=(Alice Bob Charlie)
echo "All: ${names[@]}"
echo "Count: ${#names[@]}"
echo "Index 1: ${names[1]}"

quizData.question: What does `${#arr[@]}` give you?
quizData.correctAnswer: the number of elements in the array
quizData.explanation: The `#` before the array expansion gives the length when used with `@` or `*`.

slides.title: Looping Over an Array 🔁
slides.content:
## Using for and Indices

Two common patterns:
```bash
for item in "${arr[@]}"; do ... done
for i in "${!arr[@]}"; do echo "$i: ${arr[i]}"; done
```
The second pattern (`"${!arr[@]}"`) gives the list of indices – useful for sparse arrays.

slides.title: Loop Over Array
slides.codeSnippet:
fruits=(apple banana cherry)
for i in "${!fruits[@]}"; do
  echo "$i -> ${fruits[i]}"
done

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Always quote `${arr[@]}` to prevent word splitting: `"${arr[@]}"` keeps items intact.
